body:
The national government debts of the EU’s 27 countries amounted to approximately €35,700 per resident at the end of June 2026, according to an EU Debt Map calculation. Belgium led at roughly €60,100, followed by Italy at €54,400 and France at €52,000. These are comparison measures, not personal bills.

For each country we divide official debt at 30 June by Eurostat population at 1 January 2026. The dates are six months apart; intervening population changes are not included. Both inputs were checked against official sources. The derived result is our calculation, not an indicator published by Eurostat.

The debt-per-person map and ranking instead use debt at the end of 2025 and population at 1 January 2026, matching year-end dates. This article uses June debt with the same January population. The amounts can therefore differ.

Values are rounded to €100 after division. Countries with equal displayed amounts share a rank, so Malta and Sweden share fourteenth place. The full country comparison exposes the annual inputs and ranking separately.

Why Belgium ranks first

Belgium combined approximately €719.1 billion of government debt with a population of almost 12 million. That produces around €60,100 per resident. It did not have the largest stock: France, Italy and Germany owed more in absolute euros, but spread that amount over larger populations.

Only Belgium, Italy and France exceeded €50,000 in this comparison. Austria and Finland completed the top five at around €47,600 and €45,900. Bulgaria was lowest at €5,500, followed by Estonia at €8,300 and Latvia at €11,700. The ordering belongs to these dates, not to a permanent assessment of the countries.

Germany and Greece show the limitation

Germany came to approximately €35,000 per person and Greece €34,600. Those amounts are close; their debt-to-GDP ratios were not. Germany stood at 63.4% and Greece at 140.8% of economic output.

The denominator explains the difference. Debt per person divides by population; debt-to-GDP divides by the economy’s size. Assessing capacity therefore also requires the European debt-to-GDP comparison. Neither measure alone shows interest costs, public assets or refinancing risk.

The Netherlands stood below the weighted EU result, at roughly €28,900 per resident. That figure is neither freely available budget space nor a household liability. The debt remains an obligation of the government.

How the weighted EU result is calculated

The sum of the 27 national stocks was €16,157,459.3 million, or approximately €16.16 trillion. Dividing by their combined 451,990,314 residents gives roughly €35,747. Rounded to €100, that becomes €35,700. We do not take a simple average that gives a small country the same weight as a large one.

Eurostat separately publishes consolidated EU debt of about €15.95 trillion. Loans between EU governments are removed from that aggregate. The difference from our national-stock sum is around €206.73 billion. Because this calculation compares national debt per resident, it uses the sum of countries rather than the separately consolidated EU total.

The comparison methodology explains that choice. Quarterly debt is provisional, and population data can also be revised. A further update therefore requires checking both input series, not merely changing a date.

The ranking makes large amounts easier to grasp. Judging the burden still requires economic output, interest costs and budgets. Germany and Greece show why nearly equal amounts per person can sit within very different financial circumstances.
